query: An FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy bond coat deposited from 15–45 μm feedstock does not attain the required coating thickness. For thermal-spray deposition and subsequent service as a bond coat in a thermal barrier coating system, what single intervention could overcome this thickness shortfall while preserving coating integrity and minimal as-sprayed oxidation? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, the operating and service conditions under which it should remain effective, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the average particle size of the feedstock (e.g., shifting from a 15–45 μm range to a larger, e.g., 45–75 μm range) will enable a higher deposition efficiency and yield a thicker FeCoNiCrAl bond coat, while still preserving coating integrity and keeping as-sprayed oxidation minimal.
generation.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy bond coat produced via thermal spraying using 15–45 μm feedstock, which results in a coating that is too thin for the target application.
generation.intervention: Switch the feedstock to a powder with a larger particle size distribution (for example, targeting a range of 45–75 μm) while keeping the alloy composition and spray parameters comparable.
generation.conditions: Thermal-spray deposition (e.g., APS or HVOF) under similar processing conditions (spray distance, plasma/combustion parameters, substrate preparation) as in the baseline case; service in a thermal barrier coating system’s bond coat environment where high-temperature oxidation resistance and mechanical integrity matter.
generation.structural_mediator: The larger particles have a lower surface-area-to-volume ratio, so they absorb and retain more thermal energy during flight, promoting better splat formation and layer build-up while also reducing the relative oxidation per unit mass.
generation.mechanism: Increasing the particle size increases the momentum and mass of the in-flight particles, enabling them to form thicker splats with enhanced inter-particle bonding. This improved deposition efficiency reduces the need for multiple low-mass impacts, thereby achieving greater coating thickness without exposing increased surface area to oxidative conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: The use of larger feedstock particles is expected to produce a bond coat with a significantly greater thickness compared to the baseline (15–45 μm) deposit, while maintaining similar microstructural integrity and as-sprayed oxidation levels.
generation.baseline: A bond coat produced from a 15–45 μm powder feedstock that does not reach the required thickness and is subject to moderate in-flight oxidation.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective only when other spray parameters (e.g., gas flow, spray distance, energy input) remain within optimized ranges. Excessively large particles or a too broad distribution might compromise melting uniformity or induce undesirable splashing and un-melted particles.
generation.uncertainty: The exact improvement in deposited thickness and the trade-off between particle melting and oxidation reduction are not precisely predictable without experimental quantification; effects could vary with slight modifications in spray dynamics.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a controlled thermal-spray deposition experiment using two feedstock powder distributions: the baseline 15–45 μm and an enlarged 45–75 μm range. Keep all other process parameters (spray distance, plasma/combustion settings, substrate preparation) identical. After deposition, prepare cross-sectional samples for measurement.
measurements: Phase composition and oxidation state (using XRD and EDS mapping)
Coating adhesion and microstructural integrity (via mechanical testing and optical microscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the deposit made with the larger (45–75 μm) feedstock does not yield a statistically significant increase in coating thickness relative to the 15–45 μm baseline, or if it exhibits a notable increase in oxidation or compromised coating integrity, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Cold-sprayed AlFeNiCoCr alloy retains the same BCC structure as was observed in the powder []. In contrast, in the plasma-sprayed coating of the same composition, the FCC phase is observed as the major one []. cited_evidence.text: In this study, the powder milled for 10 h was chosen as a feedstock to deposit the coating by atmospheric plasma spraying. Prior to spraying, the feedstock powder was dried in an oven at 200 °C for 3 h to remove the moisture and improve its flowability. First, 316 stainless steel cylindrical specimens with dimensions of Φ 25 × 7 mm were used as substrates. Before spraying, the substrates were cleaned with an ultrasonic cleaner in acetone for 10 min, and then dried with a dryer. To improve the bonding strength of the coating, sand blasting one side of the substrate was carried out to obtain a certain cleanliness and roughness. During sand blasting, an Al2O3 particle with a size of less than 1.25 mm was used as an abrasive. The substrates were sandblasted under a compressed air pressure of about 0.5 MPa for 30 s. An APS system (3710, PRAXAIR SURFACE TECHNOLOGIES, Indianapolis, IN, USA) with a high-energy plasma gun (SG-100) was employed to deposit the coating. During spraying, argon was used as a primary gas, and nitrogen was used as a secondary gas, whose pressures were 0.4 and 0.3 MPa, respectively.
